name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: CrewAI: Python Framework for Orchestrating Role-Playing AI Agents
answer: CrewAI is an open source Python framework for orchestrating role-playing autonomous AI agents, made by CrewAI Inc. and released under the MIT licence. It sits in the agent orchestration layer, above language models and tools, letting developers define agents with roles, goals and backstories, assign tasks, and run crews or deterministic Flows. The one thing to know is that it targets production multi-agent automation, not just demos, so teams should expect to manage model choice, token cost, observability and governance from the start.

sections.body: CrewAI is an open source Python framework maintained by CrewAI Inc. under the MIT licence, with its repository at crewAIInc/crewAI and its official site at crewai.com. The facts held here do not record a first release date, but the repository was active as of 1 October 2026 and had 59,272 stars, so it is a current project rather than an archived one. Its own description calls it a framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, and the site describes it as an open source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above language models and tools. It is not a model, a training library or a serving runtime in the narrow sense. Instead it coordinates agents that have roles, goals and backstories, assigns them tasks, and runs them as a crew or as a Flow. The site frames this as collaborative intelligence, where agents use tools, process tasks and interact to reach complex objectives. In practice that places CrewAI alongside other agent frameworks rather than beside PyTorch or TensorFlow, because its job is to organise reasoning and tool use, not to train weights.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: CrewAI is used for multi-agent task automation where work needs reasoning, unstructured data, API or tool calls, and several specialised agents. The site's examples include a researcher agent that searches the web with SerperDevTool, a task that asks for a three paragraph report on emerging technologies, and a crew that runs sequentially and returns the report. Other pages describe production automations for research, analysis, drafting and review, documentation writing with NVIDIA NIM and Meta's Llama 3.3, and sales research at DocuSign that cut hours to minutes while raising email engagement. The framework is strongest when a team wants role-based crews with specialists, shared memory and handoffs, and when it needs a production path with tracing, guardrails and the Agent Management Platform. It is also positioned for cognitive, language-heavy automation rather than deterministic UI workflows, where the site says RPA platforms such as Automation Anywhere remain the better fit. It is not presented as a training framework, a data labelling tool or an edge inference runtime. Its inference role is to call language models, including Cerebras and NVIDIA hosted models, and to coordinate what those models do.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The entry curve is moderate for a working Python developer. The official site's Cerebras tutorial installs crewai and crewai-tools, stores an API key in a .env file, defines an agent with role, goal and backstory, defines a task with description and expected output, creates a crew with a sequential process, and calls kickoff. That is enough to get a first multi-agent workflow running, and the site offers a developer portal, an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file for agent-ready documentation. The practical prerequisites are Python, comfort with environment variables and API keys, and a basic understanding of how language models respond to prompts. The site does not state a mathematics prerequisite, and none is needed for the tutorial path. Production work is harder. Flows require state management, conditional branching, custom business logic and runtime modification, and the site argues that production systems must be observable, governable, cost-controlled, auditable and maintainable. A beginner can start from the tutorials, but an engineer moving to production should expect to learn architecture and cost control as well as the API.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: CrewAI's ecosystem is Python-first and integration-heavy. The site documents crewai-tools, a developer portal, an MCP server and llms-full.txt, and it shows integrations with Cerebras inference, NVIDIA NIM microservices and NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Model examples include Cerebras hosted Llama 3.1 8B and 70B, Meta's Llama 3.3, and the token spend article refers to Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini Pro, Haiku and 4o-mini as models teams choose between. Tool use is shown through SerperDevTool for web search. The repository has 59,272 stars in the facts held here, while an older site page cites 40,000 GitHub stars, so the star count has moved. The site also claims 60 percent of the Fortune 500, 1.4 billion agentic automations on one page and 1.7 billion agentic workflows on another, and it links a survey of more than 4,500 professionals. Those are vendor-published figures. The pages read do not describe a formal community governance model, a contribution guide or a release cadence, so those questions remain open from this material alone.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: CrewAI is built for both quick experiments and production, but the two modes have different costs. A prototype can be a short Python script with an agent, a task, a sequential crew and kickoff, and the site's tutorial shows that path clearly. Production adds Flows, which the site describes as a deterministic backbone with a thin code layer, flexible decorators, state management, conditional branching and custom business logic. It also adds tracing, guardrails, the Agent Management Platform, observability, governance, auditability and maintainability. The performance question is mostly about tokens and control. The site warns that extended reasoning can consume 20,000 to 50,000 tokens before a 500 token answer, that a ten step agent run with a 30,000 token prompt can reach 500,000 to 2 million tokens, and that RAG pipelines, tool schemas and few shot examples can drive 50,000 to 200,000 input tokens per call. It estimates that 60 to 80 percent of enterprise token spend goes to use cases that have not proved business value. So CrewAI can be fast to prototype, but production speed and memory control depend on model choice, Flow design and token discipline rather than on the framework alone.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site presents CrewAI as widely adopted in large enterprises. It claims 60 percent of the Fortune 500, names PwC and Parloa as production users, and describes DocuSign using its architecture to cut sales research time from hours to minutes. A CrewAI survey of 500 C level executives and senior leaders at organisations with more than 100 million dollars in revenue and 5,000 or more employees across seven regions reports that 100 percent plan to expand agentic AI use, 81 percent have fully adopted or are actively scaling it, 65 percent already use AI agents, and organisations have automated 31 percent of workflows on average, with a further 33 percent expansion expected in 2026. Security and governance top evaluation factors at 34 percent, while data readiness at 35 percent and insufficient talent at 33 percent are the leading obstacles. IT reports the highest impact at 52 percent, followed by Operations at 44 percent. For a developer or manager, that points to current demand for agent orchestration, Flow design, guardrails, observability and token cost skills. The survey is vendor-published, so it should be read as directional rather than independent. The active repository and MIT licence support the view that CrewAI is a current choice, not a legacy one.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: CrewAI is a Python framework, and its natural companions are language model APIs, tool APIs and enterprise systems. The site shows it calling Cerebras inference, NVIDIA NIM microservices and Meta Llama models, and it discusses model choices across Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini Pro, Haiku and 4o-mini. It uses tools such as SerperDevTool and exposes an MCP server and llms-full.txt for agent-ready documentation. In the wider market, the site compares CrewAI with Microsoft Agent Framework, AutoGen, MetaGPT and Automation Anywhere. The polyglot pattern is a Python orchestration layer that sits above model providers and tools, calls them through APIs, and coordinates agents that may read from existing systems and data sources. Microsoft Agent Framework is presented as the choice for .NET and Azure centric stacks, while Automation Anywhere is presented as the RPA choice for deterministic UI and legacy system automation. Many enterprises are said to use RPA for deterministic UI workflows and CrewAI for cognitive, language-heavy automations. CrewAI is not a replacement for a language runtime or a model server, and the site does not claim it is.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: CrewAI's limits start with scope. It is not a training framework, not a general RPA platform and not a deterministic UI automation tool, and the site itself says RPA remains better for those jobs. Its production story depends on architecture, and the site argues that most implementations are either too rigid or too loose, which means the framework does not remove the need for careful design. Token cost is a real risk, with the site's own figures showing how quickly agent runs can consume large numbers of tokens. The official material does not settle several questions. It does not give a first release date, a formal mathematics prerequisite, a detailed security model, independent latency or reliability benchmarks, pricing or licensing details for the Agent Management Platform, or a clear statement of which production features are in the open source core. Its adoption figures vary between pages, with 1.4 billion automations on one page and 1.7 billion workflows on another, and 40,000 GitHub stars on an older page against 59,272 in the facts held here. The survey is vendor-published. Those gaps should be checked against the repository and current documentation before a team commits.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
